section.title: The Birth of Moses
section.sectionRationale: A single self-contained scene, framed by the death sentence of chapter 1:22 and the flight of chapter 2:11. It follows one family's quiet defiance and God's providence hiding the deliverer in plain sight, inside Pharaoh's own household.
section.thesis: Under the shadow of a death decree, God preserves the deliverer of His people through the faith of a mother, the courage of a sister, and the unlikely compassion of Pharaoh's own daughter.
section.frameNote: One scene in three movements: a mother hides her son, then sets him afloat; a sister watches and intervenes; Pharaoh's daughter draws him out and names him Moses.

verses.text: Now a man of the house of Levi married a daughter of Levi,
and she conceived and gave birth to a son. When she saw that he was a beautiful child, she hid him for three months.

But when she could no longer hide him, she got him a papyrus {{tebah|basket}} and coated it with tar and pitch. Then she placed the child in the basket and set it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.
And his sister stood at a distance to see what would happen to him.
Soon the daughter of Pharaoh went down to bathe in the Nile, and her attendants were walking along the riverbank. And when she saw the basket among the reeds, she sent her maidservant to retrieve it.
When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the little boy was crying. So she had compassion on him and said, “This is one of the Hebrew children.”
Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?”
“Go ahead,” Pharaoh's daughter told her. And the girl went and called the boy's mother.
Pharaoh's daughter said to her, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay your wages.” So the woman took the boy and nursed him.
When the child had grown older, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him {{moshe|Moses}} and explained, “I drew him out of the water.”

tebah.gloss: Basket or ark. The very same Hebrew word is used only here and for Noah's ark in Genesis 6 to 9. As Noah's ark carried a remnant safely through judgment waters, this small tebah carries the future deliverer safely through Pharaoh's decree of death.

moshe.gloss: Moses, from the Hebrew verb mashah, to draw out. Pharaoh's daughter names him for what she did, drawing him from the water, not knowing she is naming the man who will one day draw an entire nation out of the waters of the Red Sea.

basic.context: This is the birth story of Moses, the man God will use to lead Israel out of slavery. Pharaoh has ordered every Hebrew baby boy thrown into the Nile, but a Levite mother hides her son, then sets him afloat in a waterproof basket. Pharaoh's own daughter finds him, has compassion, and raises him as her own.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history, not a fable, and it reads like one of the great providence stories of the Bible: everything that could go wrong for this baby instead works together to save him, with no miracle mentioned, only ordinary people making choices under God's unseen hand.
basic.originalLanguages: The basket is a tebah, the same word used only for Noah's ark, a small vessel that carries someone safely through judgment waters. And the name Moses comes from a Hebrew verb meaning to draw out; the one drawn from the water becomes the one who draws his people through the water.
basic.typology: The tebah quietly echoes Noah's ark, both vessels preserving God's chosen line through deadly water. Moses being rescued from a death decree over infant boys sets a pattern that recurs when Jesus, too, escapes a king's slaughter of infants as an infant Himself.
basic.christ: Moses becomes the Old Testament's great deliverer, and the New Testament repeatedly presents Jesus as the prophet like Moses, Acts 3:22, and a greater deliverer than Moses, Hebrews 3:3. Both survive an infant death decree by a ruthless king; both are preserved to lead God's people out of bondage.
basic.god: God is not named once in this account, yet His providence is unmistakable everywhere: in the mother's ingenuity, the sister's quick thinking, and the strange mercy of Pharaoh's own daughter. He works through ordinary faith and even through pagan compassion to save His appointed deliverer.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 11:23 credits Moses' parents' faith for hiding him. Acts 7:20-22 retells this history in Stephen's speech. Matthew 2:13-15 shows Jesus escaping a similar infant slaughter under Herod.
basic.oneStory: This is the hidden hinge of the exodus: the deliverer is preserved as a baby so that he can later lead the deliverance of his people. It anticipates the pattern completed in Jesus, who is also preserved from a king's murderous decree to become the true and final deliverer.

context.literary:
The ten verses fall into three movements that follow the child from danger to safety. Verses 1 to 4 take place in a Levite home and at the river's edge: a birth, three months of hiding, a basket, a sister watching. Verses 5 to 9 move to Pharaoh's daughter at the Nile: discovery, compassion, and the sister's bold proposal that brings the baby back to his own mother. Verse 10 closes with adoption and naming. The story begins with a mother giving her son up and ends with a princess giving him a name.

The passage is built on reversals of Exodus 1. Pharaoh commanded that every Hebrew son be thrown into the Nile, 1:22; the mother does put her son in the Nile, but in a sealed vessel among the reeds. Pharaoh's plan was to use the river as a grave; it becomes a cradle. Pharaoh's own daughter undoes his decree, and Pharaoh's household pays wages to a Hebrew slave woman to nurse the child he wanted dead. The king who tried to 'deal shrewdly,' 1:10, is outwitted by a mother, a sister and a daughter.

The whole episode is carried by women. Chapter 1 ended with two midwives who defied Pharaoh, and chapter 2 opens with three more women, a mother, a sister and a princess, all unnamed here. Men are almost absent: the father appears only in verse 1. The deliverer of Israel owes his life, humanly speaking, to five women, counting the midwives, before he ever lifts a hand.

The narration is spare and pointed. It does not name the parents, the sister or the princess, and it does not name God. It does not tell us what the mother hoped would happen. Instead it slows at key moments: the mother 'saw that he was a beautiful child,' verse 2; the princess 'opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the little boy was crying,' verse 6. Seeing drives the story, and each act of seeing leads to an act of preservation.

The passage also sets up what follows. Verse 11 jumps to Moses 'after he had grown up,' going out 'to his own people,' so these ten verses explain how a Hebrew came to be raised as an Egyptian and why the question of his identity will be so pressing.
context.historical:
The setting is the Nile under the decree of Exodus 1:22. The family is from the tribe of Levi, verse 1, and later genealogies give the parents' names as Amram and Jochebed and list an older brother, Aaron, and a sister, Miriam, Exodus 6:20 and Numbers 26:59. Jochebed's name appears to contain a short form of the divine name, a hint that the family knew the God of their fathers before He revealed Himself to Moses at the bush.

The basket was made of papyrus, which grew thickly along the Nile and was used in Egypt for boats as well as writing material. The mother coated it with 'tar and pitch,' bitumen and a plant resin, to make it waterproof. Placing it 'among the reeds' kept it from drifting into the current and put it where it was likely to be found. The spot may have been chosen with care: Pharaoh's daughter came to that part of the river to bathe, verse 5, and the sister was stationed to watch.

The princess's household is realistic. Royal women in Egypt had their own attendants and resources, and adoption of a foundling into an elite household is plausible. The arrangement with a wet nurse was a known practice in the ancient world; a child was often nursed for two or three years before being weaned. The mother is paid wages to nurse her own son, a detail that turns Pharaoh's economy of slavery upside down.

Ancient readers knew other stories of infants set adrift. The best known is a Mesopotamian legend of Sargon of Akkad, whose mother placed him in a basket of reeds sealed with bitumen and set him on a river, where he was found and raised. The similarity of the basket is real, but the difference in meaning is greater. Sargon's story explains a king's rise to power. Moses' story explains how God preserved the servant through whom He would free slaves and humble a king.
context.canonical:
The basket, tebah, links this story to the flood. As the BSB footnote points out, the word 'can also mean ark,' and it is used elsewhere only for Noah's vessel in Genesis 6 to 9. Noah's ark was coated with pitch, Genesis 6:14; Moses' basket with tar and pitch. In both, God preserves the one through whom a new beginning will come, carrying him through waters that bring death to others. Peter later connects the ark with baptism, 'in the ark a few people... were saved through water,' 1 Peter 3:20-21, and Paul says Israel was 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,' 1 Corinthians 10:2.

The 'reeds' of verses 3 and 5 are suf, the word in the name of the Red Sea, yam suf, Exodus 13:18. The child is placed among the reeds of the Nile; years later he will lead Israel through the sea of reeds, where Pharaoh's army will drown, Exodus 15:4. The river that was meant to swallow Hebrew sons becomes the first stage of the deliverer's story.

The New Testament retells the scene twice. Stephen says Moses 'was beautiful in the sight of God,' was nurtured for three months in his father's house, and when set outside was raised by Pharaoh's daughter 'as her own son,' being 'educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians,' Acts 7:20-22. Hebrews credits his parents' faith: they hid him 'because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king's edict,' Hebrews 11:23. Hebrews then adds that Moses, when grown, 'refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter,' Hebrews 11:24, the very adoption of verse 10.

Miriam, the watching sister of verse 4, reappears as 'Miriam the prophetess' leading Israel's song at the sea, Exodus 15:20-21, and Micah remembers her among the leaders God sent, Micah 6:4. Matthew's account of Jesus' infancy, with a king's slaughter of boys and a child preserved, Matthew 2:13-16, deliberately recalls this story.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wrote this story about himself, but he keeps himself passive. The baby does nothing but cry. The point is not the child's greatness but the hidden care of God who preserved him. Moses wanted Israel to understand that their deliverer did not rise by his own strength or cleverness; he was drawn out of death by others, before he could do anything at all. The one who later stood before Pharaoh owed his life to the courage of women and the providence of God.

He also wanted Israel to see how God defeats tyranny. There is no plague here, no miracle, no divine speech. The decree of Exodus 1:22 is undone by a mother's love, a sister's quick wit and a princess's pity. God works through ordinary people doing faithful, compassionate and brave things, and even through the household of the enemy. Israel in the wilderness, and later in exile, needed to know that God's rescue does not always come with fire and thunder.

Finally, he wanted Israel to feel the irony. The king who tried to destroy Israel's sons ended up raising Israel's deliverer in his own palace and paying the child's mother to nurse him. The story invites laughter at the pretensions of power and trust in the God who can turn a death decree into the means of salvation.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what one family did under a genocidal decree; it does not tell believers to set their children adrift. The details are specific to their crisis. Nor does it make the princess's adoption of a Hebrew child into a general teaching about adoption, though it shows compassion toward a vulnerable child in a positive light.

What carries forward is the example of faith acting within ordinary means. Hebrews 11:23 interprets the parents' actions as faith that refused to fear the king. The mother does not wait passively for a miracle; she hides, builds, plans and places. The sister watches and speaks at the right moment. Faith here is active, practical and risky. Believers are encouraged to act wisely and bravely in hard circumstances, trusting that God is at work in and through what they do. The story also teaches the value of compassion across boundaries of nation and power. The princess acts rightly when she takes pity on 'one of the Hebrew children,' verse 6, and her mercy is part of God's plan.

debates.question: Why does Pharaoh's daughter, an Egyptian, act so mercifully?

views.label: God's providence moving an outsider's heart
views.case: Scripture regularly shows God moving the hearts of those outside His covenant to serve His purposes, as with Cyrus in Isaiah 45:1-4 or Rahab in Joshua 2. The timing of her bath, the sight of the basket and the baby's cry all fit a providential pattern that the narrator leaves for the reader to see.

views.label: Simple human compassion for a crying child
views.case: The text gives no theological explanation, only that she saw the child crying and 'had compassion on him,' verse 6. It is a natural human response, and the narrator's restraint may be deliberate, showing that ordinary pity can be stronger than a king's decree.

views.label: A deliberate act of defiance
views.case: Some suggest that she recognised the child as Hebrew, verse 6, and chose to defy her father's command knowingly. On this view she stands beside the midwives of chapter 1 as another woman who refused to take part in murder.

debates.bearing: These readings are not exclusive. The text shows real human compassion and even courage, and the wider story shows God at work through it. God is sovereign even over the sympathies of those who do not know Him, and He uses them to protect His purposes.

debates.question: Is Moses' name Hebrew or Egyptian?

views.label: An Egyptian name with a Hebrew wordplay
views.case: An Egyptian word meaning 'son' or 'born of' appears in royal names such as Thutmose and Ahmose, and many scholars think the princess gave the child a name of that kind. The narrator then hears in it the Hebrew verb mashah, 'to draw out,' as the BSB footnote says: 'Moses sounds like a Hebrew term that means to lift out.'

views.label: A Hebrew name
views.case: Others take the name as Hebrew from the start, noting that the princess explains it in Hebrew terms, 'I drew him out of the water,' verse 10. Perhaps she learned it from the child's mother, or perhaps the narrator is simply giving its meaning in Israel's language.

debates.bearing: Either way, the narrator wants us to hear the Hebrew meaning. The name spoken by an Egyptian princess becomes a prophecy. The Hebrew form, mosheh, is an active participle, 'one who draws out,' so the name looks beyond what was done to him to what he will do for his people.

debates.question: Was the mother's plan an act of faith or of desperation?

views.label: An act of faith
views.case: Hebrews 11:23 credits the parents' faith for hiding Moses and says they were unafraid of the king's edict. The careful preparation of the basket, the chosen place among the reeds and the sister stationed to watch suggest a plan made in trust that God would act.

views.label: A desperate hope
views.case: The text says she placed him in the basket when 'she could no longer hide him,' verse 3, and it does not mention prayer or faith. Some see a mother doing the last thing she could, with no clear expectation of what would happen, which is why the sister stood 'to see what would happen to him,' verse 4.

debates.bearing: Faith and desperation are not opposites. The mother may have acted in both at once, and Hebrews shows that God counts such action as faith. The story encourages believers who act in fear and uncertainty that God can honour even trembling obedience.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 says the mother 'saw that he was a beautiful child.' The Hebrew is simply that she saw 'that he was good,' ki tov. The phrase is the one repeated in Genesis 1, 'God saw that it was good,' and the narrator may intend the echo. Stephen interprets the word as 'beautiful in the sight of God,' Acts 7:20. Something about this child is noticed as good in a world under a death sentence.

The basket, tebah, is explained by the basic text and the BSB footnote. Two further details are worth noting. The mother coats it with chemar, 'tar,' the same word used for the 'tar' the builders of Babel used instead of mortar, Genesis 11:3, and for the 'tar pits' of the valley of Siddim, Genesis 14:10. She also uses zefet, 'pitch,' a different word from the pitch of Noah's ark, but the purpose is the same: to seal a vessel against water. The ark that saved a family through the flood becomes a basket that saves a single child through Pharaoh's river.

The 'reeds,' suf, verses 3 and 5, are the plant that gave the Red Sea its Hebrew name, yam suf, literally 'sea of reeds,' Exodus 13:18. The narrator places the infant in the same vocabulary that will describe the sea through which he will lead Israel.

In verse 6 the princess 'saw the child, and behold, the little boy was crying.' The word hinneh, 'behold,' shifts the viewpoint so that we see through her eyes. The word for boy changes from yeled, 'child,' to na'ar, 'lad' or 'little boy.' Then 'she had compassion on him,' chamal, a verb that means to pity and also to spare, as in God's command not to 'spare' Amalek, 1 Samuel 15:3. Her compassion is literally a sparing of the life her father had condemned.

The name Moses, mosheh, is explained by the verb mashah, 'to draw out.' The verb is very rare. Outside this verse it appears only in David's song of deliverance, 'He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters,' 2 Samuel 22:17 and its twin, Psalm 18:16. David uses the language of Moses' rescue for his own. The form of the name is significant too. Mosheh is an active participle, 'one who draws out,' not a passive form, 'one who was drawn out.' The princess meant to describe what she had done for him; the name itself points to what he will do for Israel.

Finally, in verse 10 'he became her son,' vayhi lah leven. The phrase is the language of adoption. The Hebrew boy is formally part of Pharaoh's household. Hebrews 11:24 picks this up when it says Moses later 'refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter.' The adoption that saved his life would one day be the identity he had to renounce.

typology.type: The tebah, a vessel of salvation through deadly waters
typology.fulfillment: The only two vessels called tebah in Scripture both carry God's chosen through waters of judgment: Noah's ark through the flood and Moses' basket through Pharaoh's river. Peter sees in the ark a pattern of salvation 'through water,' fulfilled in baptism 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,' 1 Peter 3:20-21. The escalation is that Christ Himself is the true place of refuge, the one in whom believers are carried through death into new life. The type falls short because the basket and the ark saved only bodies for a time, while union with Christ saves the whole person for ever.

typology.type: The deliverer preserved from a king's slaughter of infants
typology.fulfillment: Moses was preserved as a baby from Pharaoh's decree to kill Hebrew boys, so that he could later lead his people out of slavery. Jesus was preserved as a baby from Herod's slaughter of the boys of Bethlehem, taken by night to Egypt, Matthew 2:13-16, so that He could accomplish a greater deliverance. The correspondence is close and deliberate in Matthew. The escalation is that Moses led Israel out of Egypt, while Christ leads His people out of sin and death. Moses was a servant in God's house; Christ is the Son over it, Hebrews 3:3-6.

typology.type: The one drawn out who draws others out
typology.fulfillment: Moses was drawn out of the water and became the one who drew his people out through the sea. His life began with a rescue from death that anticipated the rescue he would lead. Christ was not merely drawn out of water; He was raised out of death itself, and through His resurrection He draws His people out of death with Him, Romans 6:4. He said, 'I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself,' John 12:32. The type falls short because Moses was himself a sinner in need of rescue, while Christ drew others out as the sinless Son.

typology.type: The adopted son who refused Pharaoh's house
typology.fulfillment: Moses 'became her son,' verse 10, gaining the privileges of Egypt's royal household, yet 'by faith Moses, when he was grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter,' choosing 'to suffer oppression with God's people,' Hebrews 11:24-25. Christ, who had the glory of the true Son, 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7, and chose to share the sufferings of His people. The escalation is that Moses gave up an adopted status he had received by grace, while Christ laid aside a glory that was His by right. Hebrews even says Moses valued 'disgrace for Christ' above Egypt's treasures, Hebrews 11:26.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ first by pattern, and Matthew makes the pattern explicit. Moses was born under a king's decree to kill Hebrew boys and was preserved; Jesus was born under a king's decree to kill the boys of Bethlehem and was preserved, Matthew 2:13-16. Matthew even brings Jesus to Egypt and out again, 'Out of Egypt I called My Son,' Matthew 2:15, so that the infant Jesus relives the story of Israel and of Moses. The attempt to destroy the deliverer at birth is the same enemy's strategy in both cases, the dragon of Revelation 12:4 standing before the woman to devour her child.

It leads to Christ through the office Moses would hold. Moses became Israel's prophet, mediator and deliverer, and God promised through him, 'The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers,' Deuteronomy 18:15. Peter declares that Jesus is that prophet, Acts 3:22. Hebrews says Jesus 'has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself,' Hebrews 3:3. The baby in the basket is the first chapter in the story of the man whose whole life pointed forward to One greater.

It leads to Christ by contrast. Moses was passive in his rescue; everything was done for him by others. Christ entered the world as a baby too, dependent on Mary and Joseph, but His life was a voluntary mission: 'the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. Moses was saved from the death decree; Christ went willingly to death under a death decree and rose.

It leads to Christ in the theme of identity. Moses was a Hebrew raised as an Egyptian and had to choose which people he belonged to. Hebrews says he chose 'to suffer oppression with God's people rather than to experience the fleeting enjoyment of sin,' and 'valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt,' Hebrews 11:25-26. Christ, the eternal Son, chose to identify with His people, becoming 'like His brothers in every way,' Hebrews 2:17, so that He could deliver them.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The basket is not a code for the manger, and the princess is not a figure of Mary. The link to Christ rests on the pattern of the preserved deliverer, which Matthew and Hebrews themselves draw, and on the office Moses held, which the New Testament says Christ fulfils and surpasses.
study.god:
God is not named once in these ten verses, and that silence is itself a teaching about Him. He is the God who works through ordinary means. There is no angel, no dream, no voice from heaven. Yet by the end of the story it is impossible to miss His hand: the right place among the reeds, the right time for the princess to bathe, a crying baby, a quick-witted sister, and a mother paid to nurse her own son. The doctrine of providence, that God governs all things for His purposes through ordinary causes, is shown here rather than stated.

He is sovereign over the powers that oppose Him. Pharaoh's decree was the policy of the most powerful state in the world. God does not overturn it with force; He simply routes His purpose through it. The river becomes the place of rescue, and Pharaoh's household becomes the place where the deliverer is raised. Psalm 2:4 says of the rulers who plot against Him, 'The One enthroned in heaven laughs', and this story has that laughter in it.

He is the God who preserves life. Chapter 1 ended with a decree of death; chapter 2 begins with a birth and moves toward adoption. God's purpose is to save, and even under a regime of death He protects the vulnerable. His care reaches a single baby in a basket, and it is exercised through the love of a mother and the compassion of a stranger.

He works through those outside His covenant people. Pharaoh's daughter did not know the God of Israel, yet her pity served His purpose. God's sovereignty extends to the hearts of those who do not know Him, and His goodness can be seen in their kindness. This does not make them members of His people, but it shows that He is the Lord of all, not merely the God of one nation.

He is faithful to His promises. God had said to Abraham that He would judge the nation that enslaved his descendants and bring them out, Genesis 15:14. The birth of Moses is the first visible step toward that promise. God does not forget His word, even when His people are in the depths of slavery and He appears to be silent.

For worship, the passage invites believers to trust God's hidden hand in the ordinary events of life, to act faithfully without waiting for visible miracles, and to take heart that the God who saw a baby in the reeds sees His people in every danger.

crossReferences.note: God commands Noah to make an ark and 'coat it with pitch inside and out.' The same word, tebah, is used for Moses' basket, which is also coated to keep out the water. Both vessels preserve God's chosen through waters that bring death to others.

Pharaoh's decree that every Hebrew son be thrown into the Nile. The birth of Moses must be read against it: the mother places her son in the Nile, but in a sealed basket, and the river of death becomes the place of rescue.

The genealogy that names Moses' parents as Amram and Jochebed, both of the tribe of Levi. The anonymous 'man of the house of Levi' and 'daughter of Levi' in Exodus 2:1 are identified, and the priestly tribe's link to Moses and Aaron is established.

Miriam the prophetess leads the women in song after the crossing of the sea. The sister who watched the basket among the reeds, Exodus 2:4, now celebrates as Pharaoh's army lies in the sea, 'the horse and rider He has thrown into the sea.'

David sings, 'He drew me out of deep waters,' using the rare verb behind the name Moses. David takes the language of Moses' rescue from the Nile and applies it to his own deliverance from his enemies, making it part of Israel's language of praise.

Stephen's retelling: Moses was 'beautiful in the sight of God,' nurtured three months at home, and raised by Pharaoh's daughter 'as her own son,' being educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Stephen uses the story to show God preparing a deliverer whom Israel would reject.

Hebrews credits the faith of Moses' parents, who were unafraid of the king's edict, and then notes that Moses, when grown, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter. The adoption of Exodus 2:10 became an identity Moses gave up by faith.

Joseph takes the infant Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod, who then kills the boys of Bethlehem. Matthew shapes the story to recall Moses: a king's decree against infants, a child preserved, and a deliverer who will lead his people out.

Peter says that in the ark a few people 'were saved through water,' and that this water 'symbolizes the baptism that now saves you.' The tebah of Noah, and by extension of Moses, becomes a picture of salvation through Christ's resurrection.

Jesus is 'counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, just as the builder of a house has greater honor than the house itself.' The baby preserved in the basket grew into a faithful servant, but he points beyond himself to the Son who built the house.

study.oneStory:
Genesis told how God began again after judgment by preserving one family in an ark, Genesis 6 to 9. Exodus 2 tells how God begins His great work of redemption by preserving one baby in an ark. The same word, tebah, links the two. The flood showed that God would not let sin and death have the last word over His creation; the birth of Moses shows that He will not let a tyrant have the last word over His people.

The passage answers the crisis of Exodus 1. Pharaoh has decreed death for every Hebrew son, and the promise of a multiplying people seems about to be crushed. The enmity of Genesis 3:15 is at its sharpest: the seed of the serpent against the seed of the woman. Exodus 2 is God's first answer, not a thunderbolt but a baby, preserved through the courage of women and the providence of God.

It sets up everything that follows. The child drawn from the water will grow up, flee, meet God at the burning bush, confront Pharaoh, lead Israel through the sea and receive the law at Sinai. He will be the mediator of the covenant and the prophet through whom God speaks. Much of the Old Testament's story, from Exodus to Deuteronomy, is his story.

The story comes to rest in Christ. Moses was preserved from a king's decree to become Israel's deliverer; Jesus was preserved from a king's decree to become the world's Saviour. Moses led Israel out of Egypt; Jesus accomplishes an exodus from sin and death, Luke 9:31. Moses was a servant in God's house; Jesus is the Son over it, Hebrews 3:5-6. 'The law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,' John 1:17.

The new creation completes the pattern. Revelation pictures the redeemed standing beside a sea, singing 'the song of God's servant Moses and of the Lamb,' Revelation 15:3. The deliverance that began with a baby in a basket among the reeds ends with a people who have passed through every danger, safe in the presence of God, praising Him for a rescue that Moses' life only foreshadowed.

quiz.q: Why did Moses' mother place him in a basket on the Nile rather than continuing to hide him at home?

options.text: Pharaoh commanded her to do it.
options.note: Pharaoh's command was to kill Hebrew sons; this mother acted against that command, not because of it.

options.text: She could no longer hide him and trusted God with a costly, faith-filled plan.
options.note: Verse 3 says she acted when she could no longer hide him; Hebrews 11:23 credits this to faith.

options.text: She wanted to abandon him permanently.
options.note: The careful waterproofing and the sister's watch show this was a rescue plan, not abandonment.

options.text: She had no plan at all.
options.note: The waterproofed basket and the watching sister show a deliberate, careful plan.

quiz.q: What role did Moses' sister play in the story?

options.text: She reported the family to Pharaoh.
options.note: The opposite is true; she acted to protect and provide for her brother.

options.text: She played no part in the story.
options.note: Her watching and quick thinking are central to how Moses came to be nursed by his own mother.

options.text: She rescued him from the water herself.
options.note: It was Pharaoh's daughter's maidservant who retrieved the basket; the sister then intervened afterward.

options.text: She watched from a distance and cleverly arranged for their own mother to nurse him.
options.note: Verses 4 and 7 to 8 show her watching, then offering to find a nurse, resulting in her mother's care and pay.

quiz.q: How did Pharaoh's daughter respond when she found the baby?

options.text: She obeyed her father's decree and had him thrown back into the river.
options.note: She did the opposite, adopting and raising him as her own son.

options.text: She ignored the child entirely.
options.note: She actively retrieved the basket and took responsibility for the child.

options.text: She was angry at the Hebrews for the child's presence.
options.note: Her response was compassion, not anger.

options.text: She had compassion on him even though she recognized he was a Hebrew child.
options.note: Verse 6 explicitly says she had compassion and identified him as a Hebrew child.

quiz.q: What does the name Moses mean, and why is it given?

options.text: It was simply a common Egyptian name with no meaning given.
options.note: The text explicitly explains the meaning behind the name.

options.text: It means prince of Egypt.
options.note: This is a common misconception; the text explicitly ties the name to being drawn from the water, not to royal status.

options.text: It means drawn out, because Pharaoh's daughter drew him from the water.
options.note: Verse 10 gives this explanation directly, from the Hebrew verb mashah, to draw out.

options.text: It means the one who will die in the water.
options.note: The naming is about rescue from water, not death by it.

quiz.q: What is the main theological point of this chapter, given that God is never named in it?

options.text: The events were pure coincidence with no theological weight.
options.note: Scripture consistently treats such providential rescues as purposeful, not accidental.

options.text: God's providence preserves His purposes through the ordinary faith and courage of unnamed and even unbelieving people.
options.note: The absence of miracles or divine speech highlights providence working through human choices, including Pharaoh's own daughter.

options.text: Moses saved himself by his own cleverness as an infant.
options.note: Moses was an infant with no agency; the rescue came through his family and Pharaoh's daughter, under God's unseen hand.

options.text: God was absent from this situation.
options.note: The chapter's placement in the whole exodus narrative, and Hebrews 11:23, show God was very much at work, even unnamed.

questions: Moses' mother acted in faith when she could no longer hide her son. Where is God asking you to release something you cannot control into His hands, trusting Him with the outcome?
God used the compassion of an Egyptian princess, someone entirely outside His covenant people, to protect His purposes. Where have you seen God work through unexpected people to accomplish His will?
This chapter never names God, yet His providence is unmistakable. Where in your own story can you now see God's hidden hand at work, even though it did not feel like it at the time?
Moses was named for being drawn out of the water, and he later drew his whole people through the sea. How has God used something painful in your past to shape you for a purpose you could not yet see?
A sister's quick thinking reunited a mother with her child. What small, courageous action might God be asking of you today, whose full significance you may not see for years?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word for basket, tebah, is the same word used for Noah's ark in Genesis 6:14, a deliberate echo of a vessel that preserves life through deadly water.
Moses sounds like the Hebrew verb mashah, to draw out, though as an adopted child his name may also carry an Egyptian root; the text gives the Hebrew meaning as the reason for the name.
